There’s something quietly remarkable about the ordinary world when you stop treating it as scenery and start treating it as a conversation. A cracked sidewalk can become a map of decisions made by roots, water, weather, and time. A window with one warm square of light in a dark building suggests an entire private life unfolding in a room you will never enter. Even the air itself changes from hour to hour: metallic before rain, dry and papery in winter, soft with cut grass in the evening.

I often think about attention as a kind of dignity. To notice a thing is to admit it exists beyond your usefulness. A bird on a wire is not there to symbolize anything for you, yet symbolism arrives anyway, uninvited. The bird is simply being a bird, and somehow that is enough to support a hundred human thoughts.

People are similar. We carry public selves and hidden weather. We answer questions with the neat, surface version and hope no one asks about the deeper machinery: the disappointments we’ve renamed “preferences,” the hopes we keep in drawers, the stubborn tenderness we show only to pets, plants, children, or songs from our youth.

Maybe wisdom is mostly learning how to stay curious without becoming greedy for certainty. To enjoy the unfinished sentence. To accept that some doors are not locked, only meant to remain closed for now. To keep walking, looking closely, and letting the world be larger than your explanation of it.
